newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler cost-cutting extends to capital spending.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler cost-cutting extends to capital spending.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. has extended its war on costs to its capital expenditure budget, although the cuts are not expected to affect future product programmes, company officials and analysts said Wednesday.

Furman Selz analyst Maryann Keller said in a research note the No. 3 U.S. automaker plans to trim $1 billion from its spending budget over the next few years in response to slowing sales and increased competition.

Chrysler spokesman Steve Harris said the company has not launched a specific plan to cut its capital spending, which was $4.64 billion in 1996. But he said the expenditures are included in the company's renewed emphasis on cost-cutting.

"We definitely have ratcheted up the effort in the last 30 to 60 days based on the weakness of the market," he said. "But only to the point where it doesn't impact future product programmes or quality initiatives."
Other recent actions include a company-wide hiring freeze. The company also announced it has identified $1.2 billion in new cost savings from suppliers for the 1997 model year.
Chrysler, facing comparisons to record sales a year ago, has experienced larger monthly drops than other members of Detroit's Big Three.

The company's May sales were down nearly 16.6 percent, while the total industry fell 5.8 percent. For the first five months of this year, Chrysler's light vehicle sales were off 7.3 percent, compared to a 1 percent decline for the whole industry.

Keller said Chrysler's June light vehicle sales are likely to fall 20 percent from a year ago. Harris said June sales will be down from last year's record high but he declined to provide a specific amount.

Because of slowing sales, rising incentives and reduced production, Keller said she has lowered her 1997 earnings estimate for Chrysler to $4.07 a share from $4.53. For all of 1996, Chrysler earned $4.77 a share, or $3.53 billion.

"Although Chrysler is a relatively efficient developer and assembler of vehicles, increased capacity in light trucks and more competition from the Japanese is challenging the ability of the company to maintain historic margins," Keller wrote.

As a result, she said, margin expansion is likely to come more from cost cutting than price hikes or market share gains. In the last week, seven analysts have slashed their second-quarter and full-year 1997 estimates for Chrysler, according to First Call Corp.
Last week, Chrysler set a third-quarter production schedule with 7.1 percent fewer vehicles than the 1996 third period. It also slightly reduced its second-quarter output forecast.
Chrysler's stock was unchanged at $32.625 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
